entry.title: The depreciation results differ between the two currencies - SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition
entry.content:
After running depreciation, upon comparing the Company Code currency and Global Currency, the exchange rate did not use the one defined by the customer.

The depreciation run does NOT translate the posting amounts for the individual currencies. In fact the currency translation takes place for the asset acquisition posting with the given posting parameters (posting date, etc.).

For example, an asset has the initial acquisition posting in period 11. The acquisition posting was done with 26,500.00 MYR

(= Company Code Currency). This posting amount was translated to 5,640.70 USD (= Group Currency).

Once the acquisition is posted, the system then calculates the depreciation amounts for each currency type (Currency Type = Company Code Currency or Group Currency).

The depreciation parameters for this asset in depreciation area 01 are currently:

  • Depreciation Key: LINK (= APC over Useful Life)
  • Useful Life: 10 Years and 0 Periods

Hence the system calculates the following depreciation amounts:

  1. Company Code Currency (MYR)

Depreciation 2023 = 26,500 MYR x 10% [= 1/10] x 2 / 12 [2 periods pro rata for periods 11 & 12]
= 441.67 MYR

As the rounding setting is set to round the net book value, this calculated amount is adjusted to 442.00 MYR.

  1. Group Currency (USD)

Depreciation 2023 = 5,640.70 USD x 10% [= 1/10] x 2 / 12 [2 periods pro rata for periods 11 & 12]
= 94.01 USD

As the rounding setting is set to round the net book value, this calculated amount is adjusted to 94.00 USD.

As shown above, the currency translation does not take place at the time of the depreciation posting. This is necessary so that the (original) APC is distributed evenly over the useful life. If the currency translation were to take place at every depreciation posting, it could not be ensured that the net book value reaches zero at the end of the useful life.

The amounts in different currencies can be viewed in the app "Manage Fixed Asset". In the valuation section for depreciation area 01, there is a dropdown list in the upper right corner of the value display control, in which the individual currency types can be selected.

entry.title: BTPEA Is Now Available in China: Bringing Consumption-Based Flexibility to SAP BAIP Customers
entry.content:
SAP BTP Enterprise Agreement (BTPEA) was officially released in China on May 21, 2026 (SKU 8016044), bringing a consumption-based commercial model to SAP BAIP customers in the China market.

Why Is BTPEA in China an Important Milestone?

The launch of BTPEA in China marks an important step in expanding the commercial options available to SAP BAIP customers, creating opportunities to onboard more services into the local portfolio, and providing greater flexibility in how customers consume SAP BAIP services.

1. Introducing a Consumption-Based Commercial Model to China

Before BTPEA became available in China, Subscription was the only commercial model available to SAP BAIP customers in the China market. The introduction of BTPEA expands the available commercial choices beyond subscription-based commitments.

While Subscription is well suited to predictable workloads and predefined service requirements, BTPEA provides greater flexibility for customers whose consumption needs may change over time. Customers can use prepaid cloud credits across eligible services, switch between services as business requirements evolve, and pay for actual consumption within the terms of their BTPEA contract.

This flexibility is particularly valuable for customers exploring new use cases, managing fluctuating workloads, adopting services for which long-term consumption requirements are difficult to predict, or combining predictable subscription commitments with consumption-based cloud credits for more experimental workloads.

2. Enabling a Broader SAP BAIP Service Portfolio in China

Some SAP BAIP services are offered exclusively through the consumption-based commercial model. With BTPEA now available in China, more services can be considered for onboarding into the China market. For example, the following services are consumption-based only and are now available in China through BTPEA: Kyma runtime, SAP Build Work Zone advanced edition, Task Center, SAP Forms Service by Adobe, Object Store, Transport Management, Data Privacy Integration, etc.

This creates opportunities to expand the SAP BAIP service portfolio available to customers in China and helps make the China offering more complete and aligned with the evolving global portfolio.

Ultimately, a broader service portfolio gives customers more opportunities to access SAP BAIP capabilities and select the services that best meet their business needs.

What Is SAP BTPEA?

SAP BTP Enterprise Agreement (BTPEA) is a consumption-based commercial model that allows customers to consume eligible SAP BAIP services using prepaid cloud credits.

Under this model, customers make an upfront investment in cloud credits for the contract duration, with an annual commitment to consume SAP BAIP services. The cost of actual consumption is deducted from the available cloud credit balance.

BTPEA is particularly suitable for customers with established business plans who need flexibility to activate and deactivate services, switch between eligible services, and accommodate changing resource requirements without committing to a single service throughout the contract duration.

Key benefits include:

  • Flexibility: Switch between eligible SAP BAIP services as business requirements evolve.
  • Consumption transparency: Receive a monthly balance statement detailing service consumption and the corresponding costs.
  • Simplified commercial management: Use prepaid cloud credits across eligible services instead of managing separate subscription commitments for every service.
  • Volume-based discounts: Benefit from volume-based discounts, subject to the applicable commercial terms.
  • Access to an evolving service catalog: Access new SAP BAIP services as they become available under the consumption-based commercial model.

Customers are billed annually in advance. Any consumption exceeding the available cloud credit balance is billed in arrears at list price. Customers can purchase additional cloud credits at any time to help prevent overages.

BTPEA in China: Service Availability

Service availability varies by country, region, and contract terms. Customers can use the following resources to check which services are available in China and review the applicable pricing information.

1. SAP Discovery Center — Service Availability and Pricing Overview

Visit SAP Discovery Center

The SAP Discovery Center provides a non-legally binding reference for service availability and pricing. Customers can filter by Regions and Commercial Model to identify services available in China under BTPEA.

China currently has two available regions:

  • China (North 3) — cn20
  • China (Shanghai) — cn40

Note that not all services are available in both regions.

2. SAP BTPEA Price List — Contractual Reference

Visit the SAP BTPEA Price List

The SAP BTPEA Price List provides legally binding contract documentation. Customers can filter by Country and Contract Start Date to check service availability and pricing applicable to their contracts.

Please refer to the applicable contractual documentation for the final commercial terms.

Combining Subscription and Consumption-Based Models with a Hybrid Account

Many customers have existing SAP BAIP subscription contracts while also needing the flexibility of consumption-based services. A hybrid account supports both commercial models within the same SAP BAIP global account, allowing customers to combine predictable subscription commitments with consumption-based cloud credits.

This approach offers several benefits:

  • Reduced administration effort: Both subscription and BTPEA contracts can coexist under the same SAP BTP global account, so development and service consumption are managed in a single environment.
  • Commit more, save more — and pay only for what you use: Lock in attractive volume discounts through subscription commitments for predictable workloads, while using BTPEA cloud credits to cover peak periods or exploration projects where resource requirements are uncertain.

How Does Charging Work in a Hybrid Account?

The charging mechanism follows the applicable subscription entitlement quota and the consumption-based model.

When customers consume services covered by their subscription entitlement quota, that consumption is covered by the subscription model. Once consumption exceeds the subscription entitlement quota, the excess consumption is charged under the consumption-based model, using the available cloud credits.

This arrangement allows customers to retain their existing subscription commitments while using BTPEA to accommodate additional consumption.

China-Specific Considerations

While BTPEA is now available in China, there are a few operational considerations customers should be aware of.

1. Cockpit Cost and Usage Visibility

The Cost and Usage tabs in SAP BAIP Cockpit are available for the consumption-based offering in China, providing customers with visibility into their consumption and related costs.

Most of the planned Cockpit functionality is available. However, the Budget module is not yet fully available in the China offering.

Customers should take this limitation into account when planning their cost-monitoring processes. Further updates will be communicated as the remaining functionality becomes available.

2. Balance Statement Email Distribution

In the global process, balance statement (BS) emails are sent directly to customers. China follows a different process due to the role of CDC.

In China, CDC acts as SAP's third-party contracting partner — customers sign contracts with CDC rather than directly with SAP. As a result, all balance statement emails would be routed to CDC first, for centralized translation and forwarding to customers.

Key Resources You Should Know

The following resources are essential reading for getting started with BTPEA — covering the consumption-based commercial model, consumption monitoring, and balance statement verification.

  • SAP Help Portal: What Is the Consumption-Based Commercial Model? — Learn about the principles and benefits of the consumption-based commercial model.
  • SAP Help Portal: Monitoring Usage and Consumption Costs in Your Global Account — Understand how to monitor service usage and consumption costs.
  • SAP Learning: Verifying the Balance Statement — Learn how to review and verify balance statements.
  • SAP Document: FAQ Consumption-Based Commercial Model CPEA & Cloud Credits — Find answers to frequently asked questions about consumption-based commercial models and cloud credits.

entry.title: Handling Reversals and Cancellations in SAP Logistics Management
entry.content:
Reversals and Cancellations in Logistics Management

Logistics rarely runs in a straight line. A customer cancels an order hours after the picking team has already started. A carrier rejects a freight assignment at the last minute. A supplier delivers fewer items than expected. A data entry error slips through master data and propagates all the way into a warehouse task. These are not edge cases — they are part of daily operations in any distribution or manufacturing environment.

What makes the difference is whether your logistics system can handle them gracefully, or whether your team is left improvising. SAP Logistics Management (LGM) is built with exactly these situations in mind. It provides a structured, end-to-end set of rejection, cancellation, and reversal capabilities that let your team correct mistakes, halt unwanted shipments, and synchronize changes back to SAP S/4HANA — without leaving the system.

 

Outbound Process: Integration and the Sequential Reversal Model

SAP LGM is tightly integrated with SAP S/4HANA. Outbound deliveries created in S/4HANA are replicated to SAP LGM, where they become logistical demands — the central documents that drive transportation requests, warehouse requests, consignments, and pickup documents.

 

This integration means that every cancellation or reversal in SAP LGM has a corresponding impact in S/4HANA. The system enforces a sequential reversal model: you can only cancel or reject a process step if all downstream steps have already been reversed first. The further along the process a shipment has progressed, the more steps need to be unwound before the underlying demand can be cancelled.

The principle is straightforward — work backwards:

  1. Reverse transport execution first (if active)
  2. Then reverse warehouse execution
  3. Then cancel transportation planning steps
  4. Then cancel the logistical demand or delivery

 

Outbound Delivery: Declining, Cancelling, and Adjusting

For outbound processes, SAP LGM offers three distinct levers depending on how far processing has progressed.

 

Decline Outbound Delivery

When an integration task arrives with errors — due to master data issues or a customer cancellation shortly after distribution — the Monitor Integration Tasks app lets you decline the delivery at any time. No prerequisites apply. The system marks the task as Declined and creates a new task to communicate the decline back to the outbound delivery in SAP S/4HANA.

 

Cancel Logistical Demand

Once a logistical demand exists in the system, it can be cancelled from the Monitor Logistical Demands app, provided processing has not advanced beyond certain thresholds. Cancellation is always possible for demands with errors. For demands that are in progress, the consignment must not be in tendering, must not have been sent to SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration, warehouse activities must not have started, and carrier arrival must not have been confirmed. If any of those conditions are not met, the corresponding steps must be reversed first.

 

Reduce Outbound Item Quantities

When a customer reduces their order after the outbound delivery has already been distributed, you can reduce the item quantity directly on the outbound warehouse request in the Manage Outbound Warehouse Activities app. The updated quantity is automatically communicated back to the outbound delivery in S/4HANA. This is only possible before goods issue has been posted — after that point, a goods issue reversal is required first.

 

Once carrier assignment is underway, additional cancellation steps come into play. The behavior differs significantly depending on whether transportation planning runs through SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration or not. Understanding which scenario applies is the first decision point before taking any action.

 

Scenario A: Transportation Planning with SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration

When SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration is involved, a strict constraint applies: it is not possible to cancel a delivery (ODLV/LD) as long as there is an open communication channel — either an active tender or an open subcontracting confirmation. The carrier communication must be resolved first before the underlying demand can be cancelled.

When an outbound delivery / logistical demand is cancelled and there is no open communication to SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration, the corresponding transportation documents (transportation requests, consignments) are automatically cancelled — provided that warehouse processing has not yet started. In addition, a cancellation is automatically sent to SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration.

Freight tenders can be cancelled from the Manage Freight Tendering app from three statuses: Open, Awaiting Response, or Quote Received. If the tender is in Awaiting Response or Quote Received status, a cancellation notification is automatically sent to the carrier via SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration.

 

Scenario B: Transportation Planning without SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration

When an outbound delivery / logistical demand is cancelled, the corresponding transportation documents (transportation requests, consignments, freight orders) are automatically cancelled — provided that warehouse processing has not yet started. Notifications can be activated if the user wants to be informed about the cancellation of the outbound delivery.

In a Direct LTL scenario, you can also manually cancel the transport booking request in the Manage Consignments app after the request has been sent to the carrier.

 

Warehouse Execution: The Reversal Sequence

 

Outbound warehouse activities follow a strict reversal sequence. Each step must be undone in reverse order before the previous one becomes available.

Step 1 — Cancel a Picking Warehouse Task. If a picking task is still open (not yet confirmed), it can be cancelled from the Process Warehouse Tasks app. The task is removed from any work queue or bundle, and the stock reservation on the outbound warehouse request item is released.

 

Step 2 — Confirm Warehouse Task with Reduced or Zero Quantity. When a picker discovers that the available stock does not match the system quantity, the warehouse task can be confirmed with a reduced quantity — or even zero — directly from the Process Warehouse Tasks app on desktop or from the Mobile Warehouse Management app. The system then presents two options:

  • Reduce the quantity on the outbound delivery — used when the required stock is not available anywhere in the warehouse. The updated quantity is communicated back to the corresponding outbound delivery in SAP S/4HANA.
  • Create a new picking task from a different source bin — used when the required stock exists in another location in the warehouse. The system generates a new warehouse task for the remaining quantity from the alternative bin.

Step 3 — Release Stock from an Outbound Warehouse Request. If stock has already been picked but is not yet packed, the Manage Stock app allows you to release it from the outbound warehouse request. The picking status is updated, and the stock remains on the bin where it was picked — available for reuse without any further intervention.

Step 4 — Reopen Handling Units. Closed shipping handling units (HUs) can be reopened from the Packing Work Center, as long as staging is not yet completed. For parcel processes, reopening an HU automatically cancels the associated consignment, sends a cancellation message to the carrier, and invalidates the shipping label. A new label can be printed once the HU is repacked.

 

Step 5 — Reverse Staging. When items have been incorrectly packed or damaged during loading, staging can be reversed from the Manage Outbound Warehouse Activities app, provided goods issue has not been posted and loading has not been set to Completed in the pickup document.

 

Step 6 — Reverse Goods Issue. Once goods issue has been posted, it can be reversed from the Manage Outbound Warehouse Activities app. On success, the goods issue status returns to Not Started, the lifecycle status returns to Open, and stock with its handling units is recreated in SAP LGM. If the reversal fails in SAP S/4HANA, the lifecycle status remains Completed and requires manual investigation.

 

 

Transportation Execution: Correcting Physical Activities

 

 

The pickup document tracks real-time transportation milestones. All three key milestones can be reversed from the Manage Pickups and Deliveries app, and they must be reversed in order — departure first, then loading, then arrival.

Reverse Carrier Departure. This can be performed at any time with no prerequisites — making it the natural starting point when a departure was confirmed prematurely.

 

Reverse Loading Completion. Possible as long as the carrier has not departed. In an LTL scenario without transportation planning, consignments created after loading was completed are cancelled automatically, and new ones are created when loading completion is confirmed again.

 

Reverse Carrier Arrival. Possible as long as loading has not been completed and the carrier has not departed.

Together, these three actions ensure that physical activity milestones in the system always reflect what is actually happening on the loading dock.

 

 

 

Inbound Process: Cancellations and Corrections

 

 

SAP LGM provides comparable coverage for inbound processes, whether driven by purchase orders or inbound deliveries.

Cancel Inbound Logistical Demand with Errors. When an inbound delivery or purchase order is distributed to SAP LGM and the data check fails, the erroneous logistical demand can be cancelled at any time from the Monitor Logistical Demands app. Integration tasks are created to decline the corresponding inbound delivery in S/4HANA. Before cancelling, it is worth checking whether reloading the demand after fixing the underlying data is the better option — cancellation is irreversible and requires re-creating the document in S/4HANA.

 

When a supplier delivers fewer items than ordered, the inbound warehouse request quantity can be reduced directly in the Manage Inbound Warehouse Activities app. This supports partial goods receipt — the remaining open quantity stays on the purchase order for the next delivery. To fully reject an inbound delivery item, the quantity must be manually reduced to zero as part of the operational procedure.

 

Reverse Goods Receipt (GR). Available for both purchase order-based and inbound delivery-based processes from the Manage Inbound Warehouse Activities app. When triggered, SAP LGM sends a GR reversal request to S/4HANA. The inbound warehouse request shows a "Goods Receipt Reversal In Progress" status during processing. Once complete, the purchase order status is updated accordingly. All open (unconfirmed) putaway warehouse tasks must be cancelled before initiating the reversal.

 

 

What's Coming: Planned Capabilities

Relevant capabilities are currently on the SAP LGM roadmap:

Correct Quantities after Putaway. Once all putaway warehouse tasks have been confirmed and stock has been stored in its final bin, standard goods receipt reversal is currently blocked. This planned capability is designed to allow quantity correction even after putaway is complete, communicating the corrected quantities back to SAP S/4HANA automatically. Until this capability is delivered, two workarounds are available: create a stock adjustment via the physical inventory procedure, or initiate a return delivery to vendor in SAP S/4HANA.

Warehouse Task Split. When a warehouse task is confirmed with a quantity less than originally planned, the system is planned to automatically retain the confirmed quantity on the original warehouse task and create a new warehouse task for the remaining open quantity. This ensures that outstanding stock movements are tracked and completed without requiring manual intervention to recreate missing tasks.

For more information about LGM Road Map items see SAP Road Map Explorer

Key Takeaways

SAP LGM gives operations teams and implementation consultants a robust toolkit for handling exceptions at every stage of the logistics flow. A few principles are worth keeping front of mind:

  • Every cancellation follows the sequential reversal model — always work backwards from the most advanced step.
  • Prefer reloading over cancelling whenever the underlying data can be corrected. Cancellation is irreversible.
  • Carrier communications are automated where the process supports it — cancel tender, cancel subcontracting, and parcel cancellations all trigger system-to-system notifications via SAP Business Network for Logistics.
  • Most capabilities are already available today. Correct quantity after putaway and Warehouse Tasks Split — are on the roadmap, with documented workarounds available in the meantime.

 

From my experience working with SAP LGM, the question is rarely whether the system can handle an exception. The real challenge is knowing which step to take first — and in which order. I hope this guide helps your team navigate that with confidence.

For more information about Reverse and Cancel Steps in the Outbound Process, see Reverse and Cancel Steps in the Outbound Process | SAP Help Portal.

For more information about LGM Road Map items see SAP Road Map Explorer

For Latest LGM Innovation released see What's New Viewer - SAP Logistics Management | SAP Help Portal

entry.title: SAP MEI1 Performance Issues: How I Investigated WIND Table Accumulation and Resolved the Problem
entry.content:
Introduction

Have you ever encountered a situation where SAP has the correct purchasing condition records, but MEI1 takes too long to execute or fails to update all the expected purchase order items?

I recently worked on an SAP MM issue involving transaction MEI1, where users experienced performance problems during mass purchasing document adjustments. The investigation initially focused on the execution itself, but it eventually led me to examine the worklist entries maintained in the WIND table.

In this blog, I will share how I investigated the runtime errors, what I learned about worklist management, how we identified obsolete entries with business support, and how we used standard SAP functionality to resolve the issue.

1. How the issue started

The business was using MEI1 to process mass pricing updates for existing purchase orders. The expectation was that SAP would identify the relevant purchasing documents and adjust their prices based on the applicable condition changes.

However, the execution was taking longer than expected. When users executed MEI1 in the foreground, they encountered the message:

“Error: maximum runtime exceeded.”

Some purchase order items also remained unchanged after processing.

My initial focus was on understanding why the execution was taking so long and whether the relevant condition records and document selection were correct. To investigate further, I started with the ABAP dumps in ST22.


Figure 1: Standard MEI1 execution screen and available processing options.

2. The first clue: Understanding the worklist checkbox

During the investigation, I noticed that users were unchecking the “Delete worklist after processing” option.

When this option is unchecked, SAP displays a confirmation prompt stating:

“Worklist will not be deleted after processing! Run program anyway?”

Figure 2: MEI1 confirmation prompt when worklist entries are retained after processing.

This prompted me to look more closely at how the worklist was being managed.

I realized that the important question was not simply whether the checkbox should be selected or cleared. We needed to understand how entries were being generated, which entries were still required, and why the worklist had accumulated over time.

Retaining worklist entries may be appropriate for a particular processing scenario. However, if obsolete entries remain in the table, the volume of data that needs to be managed can become a performance concern.

I therefore continued the investigation rather than treating the checkbox setting as the complete solution.

3. Digging deeper into ST22: What was causing the timeout?

To understand why MEI1 was taking so long, I checked the ABAP dumps in transaction ST22.

The runtime error list showed repeated TIME_OUT errors. When I opened the dump details, the short text indicated “Time limit exceeded.”

Analyzing the dump details

I opened the relevant dump to understand what had happened. The dump identified the standard SAP program SAPLWB2S and explained that the program had exceeded the maximum uninterrupted runtime and was terminated.

Figure 3: ST22 dump details showing program SAPLWB2S and the runtime termination.

Reviewing the error analysis

The error analysis explained that SAP terminates a program when it exceeds the permitted runtime. This prevents work processes from remaining occupied for unnecessarily long periods, for example because of lengthy database accesses or endless loops.

The dump showed a configured maximum runtime of 660 seconds in this system.

These findings confirmed that the immediate technical symptom was a runtime timeout. However, the dump alone did not establish why the processing was taking so long.

I needed to investigate the underlying worklist data to determine whether accumulated or obsolete entries were contributing to the problem.

My takeaway: ST22 helped me identify the runtime failure, but further analysis was necessary to determine the corrective action.

4. Investigating the WIND table

The next step was to investigate the WIND table, which stores worklist-related entries used by Automatic Document Adjustment.

During the investigation, I found that entries had accumulated over time. One important consideration was that a particular price and validity period could be relevant to multiple purchase orders involving the same vendor and material combination.

Therefore, a large number of WIND entries did not automatically mean that all of them were obsolete. Some entries could still be needed for pending adjustments, while others might no longer be relevant.

This was an important distinction. Simply deleting all entries to reduce the table size would not have been an appropriate approach.

I needed to establish which entries were genuinely obsolete and which still had business relevance.

5. Involving the business to identify obsolete entries

I asked the business team to analyze the relevant condition records and identify entries associated with obsolete or invalid pricing that no longer required processing.

This was an essential step because the technical team could not determine solely from the age of an entry whether the corresponding pricing adjustment was still required.

The business review helped identify the records that could be considered for cleanup. Based on this analysis and the agreed approach, we proceeded with the technical correction.

This experience reinforced an important lesson for me:

WIND table cleanup is not just a technical activity. It requires an understanding of the business pricing process and confirmation that the entries selected for deletion are no longer required.

6. The fix: Using the standard SAP report RWVKP03D

After identifying the entries eligible for cleanup, I used the standard SAP report RWVKP03D, executed through transaction SE38.

The report screen is titled “Analyzing and Deleting Change Pointers from the WIND table.”

It provides selection criteria for analyzing and deleting change pointers, including condition record number and creation date. It also provides condition-related restrictions and an option to check against document indexes in table S111.

Figure 4: RWVKP03D selection screen used to analyze and delete selected WIND change pointers.

We used the report to process the entries identified as obsolete through the analysis and business confirmation.

The important point is that we did not simply clear the entire WIND table. We used the relevant condition record information to identify the entries selected for cleanup.

After the cleanup was completed, we proceeded with MEI1 processing and validated the outcome.

The issue was resolved for the scenario under investigation. This demonstrated the value of understanding and using standard SAP functionality before considering custom development.

7. What does “Delete worklist after processing” mean in practice?

This was one of the most important lessons from the investigation.

The “Delete worklist after processing” option controls whether worklist entries are deleted after processing according to the program's logic. When it is unchecked, the user is warned that the worklist will not be deleted after processing.

However, this should not be interpreted as a universal instruction to always select or always clear the checkbox. The appropriate setting depends on the processing scenario and the applicable SAP guidance.

It is important to distinguish between the following:

  • Retaining the worklist: Entries remain available after the run, which may be necessary in a particular processing scenario but can contribute to accumulation if obsolete entries are not managed.

  • Deleting entries after processing: Entries are removed according to the program's processing logic.

  • Deleting the entire worklist: This is a broader operation and must not be confused with deleting entries associated with a completed run.

If relevant entries are removed before their associated purchasing documents have been adjusted, those documents may no longer be selected through the deleted entries.

For this reason, the checkbox should not be treated as a universal performance fix. Its behavior must be understood in the context of the processing scenario, the SAP release, and the relevant selection criteria.

8. If WIND entries are deleted, how can the worklist be generated again?

During my investigation, I also wanted to understand how SAP generates worklist entries and what happens if an entry is deleted before all relevant purchase orders have been adjusted.

In standard SAP Automatic Document Adjustment, MEI1 processes the worklist, MEI3 recompiles the purchasing document index in table S111, and MEI4 generates the worklist from change pointers when the two-step worklist-generation process is configured. These transactions serve different purposes and are not interchangeable.

The worklist-generation process depends on the system configuration:

  • When direct worklist entry creation is not active: Relevant condition changes generate change pointers, which can subsequently be processed by MEI4 to create entries in WIND.

  • When direct worklist entry creation is active: Relevant WIND entries are created when the condition change is saved. In this configuration, the separate MEI4 step is generally not required for that document category.

  • When document-index entries are missing: MEI3 can be used to recompile the purchasing document index in S111, provided the relevant configuration and prerequisites are in place. MEI3 does not recreate deleted WIND entries.

     

One important point I learned is that deleting a WIND entry does not automatically guarantee that the same entry will be recreated. A new relevant condition change can generate a new worklist entry, but simply rerunning MEI1 will not necessarily restore a deleted entry.

If worklist entries have been deleted accidentally, the recovery approach depends on the configuration. In a two-step process, MEI4 may be able to regenerate entries from change pointers that are still available for processing or reorganization, subject to the applicable selection options. If direct worklist entry creation is active, the recovery procedure needs to be assessed differently.

This is why I consider it essential to understand the configured worklist-generation process before performing cleanup. We should first confirm that the affected purchase orders have been adjusted, obtain business confirmation that the selected entries are obsolete, and then use the appropriate SAP standard procedure.

My takeaway: MEI1, MEI3, and MEI4 address different parts of Automatic Document Adjustment. Understanding their individual roles helps prevent accidental loss of worklist entries and makes troubleshooting more effective.

9. Why I would investigate standard MEI1 before proposing custom development

During troubleshooting, it is common to hear suggestions to develop a custom report using purchasing APIs such as BAPI_PO_CHANGE to update the affected purchase orders.

A custom report may be justified for a specific business requirement, but it should not be the first response to every MEI1 issue.

MEI1 is part of the standard Automatic Document Adjustment process. Its behavior involves worklist selection, document indexes, condition-change relevance, and purchasing document processing.

Updating purchase orders directly does not necessarily correct an underlying worklist or document-index problem.

Before proposing custom development, I would investigate:

  • Whether the relevant condition records are correct.

  • Whether the expected entries exist in WIND.

  • Whether the corresponding document-index entries in S111 are consistent.

  • Whether MEI1 selection criteria and processing settings are appropriate.

  • Whether obsolete worklist entries are contributing to performance issues.

  • Whether the expected purchasing document updates can be completed through the standard process.

Understanding these components can help identify the actual cause and avoid unnecessary custom development.

Custom development should be considered only after the standard functionality, configuration, and business requirements have been properly assessed.

10. Preventing the issue from recurring

Resolving the immediate incident was only part of the solution. The next consideration was how to prevent obsolete entries from accumulating again.

I recommend establishing periodic monitoring of the WIND table, reviewing the entries with the business, and identifying obsolete records using agreed selection criteria.

The business should confirm that the entries selected for removal no longer represent pending pricing adjustments. The technical team should then perform the cleanup using the appropriate SAP-supported procedure and validate the results.

The monitoring frequency should be agreed based on worklist growth, transaction volume, and business requirements. Cleanup should be controlled and documented rather than performed indiscriminately.

This approach creates a repeatable preventive process instead of waiting for performance problems to appear again.

11. My key takeaways

Looking back, the most valuable lesson was that the MEI1 runtime issue could not be addressed by looking at pricing records alone.

The investigation required me to understand how the worklist was being retained, why entries were accumulating, which records were still relevant, and how standard SAP functionality could be used to clean up obsolete entries.

My main takeaways are:

  • Correct condition records do not guarantee that every expected purchase order will be updated.

  • ST22 is an important starting point for identifying and analyzing runtime errors.

  • WIND entries must be analyzed for relevance before deletion.

  • The “Delete worklist after processing” option must be understood before changing it.

  • Business confirmation is essential when deciding whether entries are obsolete.

  • RWVKP03D provides standard functionality for analyzing and deleting selected WIND change pointers.

  • After cleanup, MEI1 results should be reconciled and validated.

  • Periodic monitoring can help prevent recurring worklist accumulation.

  • Standard SAP functionality should be investigated thoroughly before proposing custom purchasing document updates.

Conclusion

What initially appeared to be a MEI1 performance problem became an opportunity to understand the relationship between condition changes, worklist management, and automatic purchasing document adjustment.

By analyzing the runtime errors in ST22, investigating WIND, involving the business in identifying obsolete entries, and using the standard SAP report RWVKP03D through SE38, we resolved the issue without immediately replacing the standard process with custom development.

For SAP MM and Retail consultants facing similar problems, my recommendation is simple: understand how MEI1 and its worklist operate before deciding on the fix.

A structured investigation, controlled cleanup, business confirmation, and ongoing monitoring can make the solution more reliable and easier to maintain.

References

  • SAP Community: Automatic Document Adjustment – Most Common Mistakes and Questions

  • SAP Help Portal: Worklist Generation

Note: Report selection criteria and deletion behavior should be validated against the SAP release and system configuration. Always obtain appropriate business confirmation and verify the impact before deleting worklist entries in production.

entry.title: User Insights: SAP Business Data Cloud practitioners' recommendations for a trusted data foundation
entry.content:
For many organizations, analytics challenges are no longer caused by a limited access to data. The challenge is now that business data exists in too many places. Finance may operate from SAP ERP. Sales teams may rely on CRM platforms. Operational data may reside in custom applications, cloud databases, data lakes, or spreadsheets. Each system contains useful information, yet business users often spend more time locating and reconciling data than generating insights from it.

These challenges define a practitioner profile we call the Business Data Unifier.

This is the fourth article in a 4-part series examining SAP Business Data Cloud practitioner profiles identified through user reviews published on the PeerSpot peer-to-peer platform. The previous articles explored the FP&A Modernizer, the BW Modernizer, and the Business AI Builder. This final profile focuses on organizations seeking to unify SAP and non-SAP data through shared business definitions, governance, and cross-platform access.

The Business Data Unifier starts from a different challenge than the other 3 profiles. Rather than replacing a legacy warehouse or enabling machine learning, the primary objective is to establish a trusted data foundation spanning systems, business units, and cloud environments.

When integration is easy but consistency is hard

Most organizations already have mechanisms for moving data. The harder question is: does the data mean the same thing wherever it is used? Different departments frequently create their own calculations, hierarchies, and KPI definitions. Analysts spend hours validating numbers before they can begin interpreting them. Business Data Unifiers focus on reducing that friction by creating a common semantic layer that can be consumed across analytics, planning, and AI use cases.

Practitioner insight 1: Establish common business definitions before expanding use cases

Many practitioners emphasize that successful data unification begins with semantics rather than integration. Santosh Pallai, Solutions Architect at NTT DATA, describes an architecture in which business rules are modeled once within SAP Datasphere and reused across consumers:

  • “Once business logic, calculations, hierarchies, and currency conversions are modeled in Datasphere, I can reuse the same analytical models across multiple reports, dashboards, and planning stories. This improves consistency, reduces duplication, enhances performance, and simplifies long-term maintenance.”
  • Santosh Pallai, Solutions Architect, NTT DATA

For the Business Data Unifier, the lesson is straightforward: agree on definitions before multiplying use cases. If financial metrics, calculations, and hierarchies are defined independently in every environment, integration alone will not create consistency. A shared semantic layer lets teams reuse those definitions across multiple consumers rather than rebuilding them for each application.

Read PeerSpot review

Practitioner insight 2: Measure success by reducing time spent reconciling data

Many organizations justify data modernization using technical metrics. Practitioner experiences suggest business productivity may be the more meaningful measure. Niyajuddin Tiwale of DigitalTrack Solutions describes how reporting improved by approximately 30-50%, reducing the effort required to prepare and reconcile information before reporting begins.

  • “Since implementing SAP Business Data Cloud, reporting has become 30 to 50 percent faster as business data no longer needs to be manually consolidated from multiple systems.”
  • Niyajuddin Tiwale, DigitalTrack Solutions

For Business Data Unifiers, that kind of improvement is an important measure of success. Less time consolidating and validating data means more time analyzing it and supporting business decisions.

Read PeerSpot review

Practitioner insight 3: Bring financial and operational data together

Business decisions rarely depend on one category of data. Financial performance, operations, customer behavior, and supply-chain metrics often need to be evaluated together. Data unification becomes more valuable when those perspectives can be connected.

Vishal Koovaparambil, Senior Cyber Security Analyst at DigitalTrack Solutions, describes consolidating financial and operational information from multiple source systems into a unified analytical environment:

  • “We recently consolidated financial and operational data from different business systems into a unified platform, which allowed the management team to access dashboards properly and generate reports without manual data combination from multiple sources.”
  • Vishal Koovaparambil, Senior Cyber Security Analyst at DigitalTrack Solutions

The takeaway is to design unification around decisions, not systems. The value comes from creating shared visibility across operational and financial outcomes, rather than simply consolidating technology platforms.

Read PeerSpot review

Practitioner insight 4: Treat data products as reusable organizational assets

As organizations operate across SAP, hyperscalers, and external data platforms, data sharing becomes increasingly important. Practitioners consistently highlight the value of reusable data products that can be consumed across multiple environments.

Muhammad Ashar, SAP Data and Analytics Consultant at Dezert Innovation Technology Company, explains:

  • “I find that analytical agility in SAP Business Data Cloud is fundamentally about data products. In the agile framework, we have continuous delivery and cannot wait on a waterfall framework for one-by-one delivery.”
  • Muhammad Ashar, SAP Data and Analytics Consultant, Dezert Innovation Technology Company

The implication extends beyond analytics delivery. A reusable data product gives multiple consumers access to the same trusted business information instead of requiring teams to recreate integrations for each new use case. For Business Data Unifiers, the goal is not simply to connect systems but to make governed data reusable across the organization.

Read PeerSpot review

A practical checklist for the Business Data Unifier

These practitioner experiences suggest several questions for teams pursuing enterprise-wide data unification:

  • Are business KPIs defined consistently across systems?
  • Can SAP and non-SAP data be accessed through common business definitions?
  • Are data ownership and governance responsibilities clearly assigned?
  • Have semantic models been established before expanding use cases?
  • Can financial and operational information be analyzed together?
  • Are reusable data products available for multiple consumers?
  • Can data be shared across platforms without unnecessary replication?
  • How much time do analysts spend gathering and reconciling data today?
  • Does reporting preparation time decrease as adoption grows?

The objective is not simply to centralize data. It is to establish trusted business meaning that remains consistent regardless of where the data is consumed.

The broader lesson for data professionals

The practitioner stories suggest that data unification is less about moving data and more about creating shared understanding. Niyajuddin Tiwale and Vishal Koovaparambil demonstrate the business value of consolidating SAP and non-SAP information into trusted reporting environments. Santosh Pallai highlights the importance of reusable semantics and centralized business logic. Muhammad Ashar illustrates how governed data products can make trusted information reusable across platforms and consumers.

Together, these experiences point toward a common principle: organizations achieve the greatest value from SAP Business Data Cloud when they standardize business definitions, establish governance early, and make trusted data reusable across the enterprise. The measure of success is not how much data has been integrated, but how confidently that data can be reused to answer business questions.

entry.title: From Potential to Realized Value: Tracking Business Outcomes with Process Transformation Manager
entry.content:
From Potential Value to Value Realized

Value Cases enable companies to identify the value or benefits that will accrue from transformation initiatives such as automation, decreased manual work or optimization of working capital.

There are two monetary values that are especially critical:

  • Potential Value: The anticipated value that can be generated.
  • Value Realized: The value that has been realized during a certain measurement period, either through operations or calculations.

For instance, a transformation to increase automation of invoices would generate an annual Potential Value of €200,000, and a Value Realized of €65,000.

Knowing both these values gives insights into expectations vs. achievements within the time frame for each.

Value Realized Across Different Value Case Sources

The transformation value generally comes from several sources or approaches. Value Realized is now supported by SAP Signavio Transformation Manager in these different sources.

Manual Value Cases

Manual Value Cases involve the recording of benefits that have been identified through business case analysis, partner assessment, operational excellence programs, or analytics.

The user has the option of entering the Value Realized data directly into SAP Signavio Process Transformation Manager.

Value Cases from SAP Signavio Process Intelligence

SAP Signavio Process Intelligence determines business value from process performance information.

When it comes to Value Cases related to Transformation Manager programs, Value Realized, which is derived from the sources, can also be shown.

 

Adjusting and Re-Synchronizing Value Realized

Source-calculated Value may sometimes be inconsistent with an organization’s accounting practices.

For instance, SAP Signavio Process Intelligence may calculate savings in productivity from improved processes whereas the finance department uses another set of labor costs or only considers a portion of the source-calculated value.

SAP Signavio Process Transformation Manager thus enables users to manually change Value Realized for SAP Signavio Process Intelligence Value Case.

Example: Adjusting a Source-Calculated Value

Consider a Value Case for improving purchase order processing:

  • Source-calculated Value Realized: €85,000
  • Value Realized recognized by Finance: €72,000

The lead can be entered in SAP Signavio Transformation Manager in €72,000 without breaking the link to SAP Signavio Process Intelligence.

This change will not affect the source calculation and process data

Returning to the Source Value

If the organization chooses to reuse the SAP Signavio Process Intelligence calculation, the users will have the option to sync back the Value Realized amount. The option becomes available once Target or Current numbers had changed on SAP Signavio Process Intelligence side after last manual adjustment of Value Realized. 

This gives the user options between customized reporting based on the customer and source-based calculation without having to recreate the value manually.

The synchronization process syncs back the source value on SAP Signavio Transformation Manager; it does not sync back the manual adjustment to Process Intelligence.

 

Tracking Value Across a Transformation Initiative

Consider an initiative called Improve Purchase-to-Pay Efficiency, containing two Value Cases:

 

Invoice Automation

Exception Handling

Source

Process Intelligence

Manual Value Case

Potential Value

€200,000/year

€90,000/year

Value Realized

€72,000 (adjusted)

€25,000 (reported)

Illustrative figures.

Both Value Cases are used in the same project, yet they are derived from separate measures.

The transformation actors can compare both expected and actual gains at once, maintaining the setting of their calculations.

It helps to talk about the results obtained, possible opportunities, and discrepancies between the values gained through the process and accounting reports.

Getting Started

For organizations that are currently implementing Value Cases, here is how they can introduce realization tracking into their current processes:

  1. Open Initiative and check the Value Cases related to it.
  2. Check Potential Value and financial assumptions behind it.
  3. Update Value Realized by adding reported benefits or checking the amounts from the source.
  4. Adjust When Necessary and synchronize values, when needed.
  5. Perform regular reviews to evaluate outcomes and find ways for improvement.

For consistent reporting, organizations need to make sure that there is consistency in measuring time, assumptions are validated, and double counting does not occur.

Connecting Transformation Execution with Business Outcomes

The Potential Value concept helps organizations discover and prioritize opportunities. The Value Realized concept helps organizations understand the value that was created by the execution process.

SAP Signavio Process Transformation Manager helps bridge this gap by enabling Value Realized from various Value Case types, providing a unified environment for transformation management.

Process Intelligence integration allows for source-calculated value, whereas manual changes and re-syncing allow customers to report on their specific needs.

Combining all of these concepts enables organizations to connect opportunities, execution, and results.

Learn More

  • Value Analysis in SAP Signavio Process Transformation Manager
  • Manual Value Cases
  • Linked Value Cases

How does your organization track realized transformation value? Share your experiences and questions in the comments.

entry.title: Configuration to download Onboarding Documents Via Onboarding Dashboard
entry.content:
Introduction:

In SAP SF Onboarding, Candidates will upload documents if there is any personal data collection step has been configured. As a common business need, if the onboarding team wants to download and verify the documents, this post which mentions the configuration of the document download can be used. The below mentioned configuration has been tested in SF Onboarding 2.0 instance with 1H 2026 released update.

Requirement:

To download all attachments from Onboarding 2.0 dashboard for any user which has been attached in the custom MDF used for the personal data collection step.

Approach:

To facilitate this scenario following steps to be configured in the system as per the sequence, to begin with the steps we should have an access to create/edit the below MDF objects

  1. Personal Data Collection (PDC) Custom Object
  2. Attachment Field Configuration
  3. ONB2DataCollectionUserConfig

Solution:

 Step 1: Creating an Attachment Field Configuration

After creating and assigning a MDF Object in PDC step, The attachment field from the PDC Object need to be added in Manage data under “Attachment Field Configuration” one by one

While creating a new field configuration, Consider the below example:

  1. The PDC object to be selected under the Object type.
  2. Attachment field to be selected for which the field you are required to download the document for.
  3. Assign the Attachment category as “Custom New Hire” since this is going to be a new hire in further steps and these documents will be stored based on the category.
  4. Entity ID should be “cust_subjectuser” - Since this ID is used to find to which the attachments to be associated and we are linking attachments to specific Subjectuser.
  5. Module - Onboarding to be chosen.     

               

Step 2: Onb Data Collection User Configuration

After all the necessary fields created in the above step, the PDC object to be associated with the  “ONB2DataCollectionUserConfig” since this object stores the attachments linked to each user’s internal ID.

                  

Add the PDC objects in the association with below list:

  1. Type: Join by column - since we are linking the Source and destination object.

  2. Destination Object to be stored as “cust_userConfig” - whenever any attachment is added by the Onboardee that will be saved by this object against respective internal ID.

  3. Source Object: As mentioned above, the attachment to be mapped with user’s Onboarding internal ID to fetch them in the dashboard, so use “internalid” as Source Object.

  4. Visibility - Need to be editable               

        

          

Step 3: Final Result

After the above all configurations completion, we are set to start collecting the attachments from the Onboardee, which will be further visible to the Onboarding team to download and view from Onboarding dashboard under Onboarding Documents.

     

    

Conclusion:

While configuring the onboarding documents I have faced an issue where the documents were not visible in the dashboard and upon checking further I got to know that Step 2 which was mentioned above to be considered, Only when associating the PDC Object to ONB Data Collection User Configuration against Internal ID we will be able to download.

entry.title: Re: Issue Fetching Data from ANEK table using CDS views
entry.content:
Hi,

ANEK is empty on the database in S/4HANA. What SE16 shows you is not the table, it is a CDS view that SAP puts in front of it for ABAP SQL. I checked it on two S/4HANA systems, 2020 and 2023, and both behave the same way.

Why SE16 shows data and your CDS view does not

  • In DD02L, ANEK has a replacement object: FAAV_ANEK, the SQL view of the CDS view FAA_ANEK ("compatibility view for table ANEK"). ANEP, ANEA, ANLP and ANLC have the same thing: FAAV_ANEP, FAAV_ANEA, FAAV_ANLP and FAAV_ANLC.
  • FAA_ANEK builds the ANEK lines from ACDOCA, joined with BKPF and with the reporting ledger of the company code. Its first SELECT reads the real ANEK with WHERE bukrs = '0001' AND bukrs = '0002', which is never true. The comment in the source says it is there only to give the view the field types of the old table.
  • A replacement object works only for ABAP SQL reads, and SE16 reads with ABAP SQL, so it gets the redirected data. The ABAP keyword documentation, page "DDIC Replacement Objects", says that a CDS view, a database view, AMDP and Native SQL that use the table still read the table itself: "The replacement object must be accessed directly."

What I measured, row counts in one client:

  • ABAP SQL, SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anek: 20 on 2023, 197 on 2020
  • Native SQL (ADBC) on table ANEK: 0 on both
  • ABAP SQL on the CDS view FAA_ANEK: 20 and 197
  • Native SQL on its SQL view FAAV_ANEK: 20 and 197
  • ABAP SQL on FAA_ANEK_ORI, a CDS view delivered by SAP that is only "select * from anek": 0 on both. This is your case.

So the "0 entries" in the runtime properties is correct. It is the database table, and the table is empty.

What you can do

  1. In ABAP code, a plain ABAP SQL SELECT FROM anek works. The redirect does the job.
  2. If you read the HANA database directly (I saw the BW/4HANA tag, so maybe from the BW side), select from the SQL view FAAV_ANEK instead of the table ANEK. It is in the same schema as the table, and native SQL on it gave the same count as ABAP SQL on ANEK.
  3. In your own CDS view, use Faa_Anek as the data source instead of anek. It has the same field names and types. On 2023 I ran the syntax check of a view entity that selects from Faa_Anek and it had no errors (only syntax checked, not activated). It is not a released API, there is no release state for it in that system, so this is for classic ABAP on premise and not for ABAP Cloud.
  4. For a stable source, read the asset lines from the released view I_JournalEntryItem, contract C1. MasterFixedAsset, FixedAsset, AssetTransactionType, AssetValueDate, AssetDepreciationArea, AccountingDocument, PostingDate and DocumentDate are there. ACDOCA keeps asset lines per ledger and depreciation area, so filter one ledger and one area, or you will get the same document more than once. FAA_ANEK does this with the reporting ledger and the leading area. The ANEK line number LNRAN is not in I_JournalEntryItem: FAA_ANEK takes it from ACDOCA-SUBTA, and SUBTA is commented out in that view.

What I did not test: a field by field comparison between FAA_ANEK and I_JournalEntryItem, and how FAA_ANEK performs on a big ACDOCA. It is a UNION ALL with several joins and a SELECT DISTINCT, and the view is annotated with size category XL.

entry.title: Trigger External APIs with Custom Actions in SAP Sales and Service Cloud Version 2
entry.content:
Trigger External APIs with Custom Actions in SAP Sales and Service Cloud Version 2

The Use Case

Consider a utilities company managing their sales contracts in SAP Sales and Service Cloud Version 2. Their sales process involves gathering data in a guided flow in V2, which is then sent to S/4HANA to create a utility sales contract. Standard actions like Change Start Date and Change End Date are already delivered out of the box.

But what about cancelling one of those change processes? Or triggering a custom process that exists in S/4HANA but was out of scope for the standard delivery?

Previously, these scenarios had no clean answer. Now, with Custom Action API support, administrators can define custom actions on their custom service entities and expose them as buttons on the UI.

In the utilities example: after a Change Start Date action is triggered (updating the date to October 20th), the agent can now click a custom Cancel Change Start Date button — which triggers an API in S/4HANA via a CPI iFlow — and the start date reverts to October 1st(previous one). A process that previously did not exist in standard delivery, now delivered through extensibility.

How It Works

The solution has two parts:

  1. Admin configures the custom service — defines an ACTIONPARAMETERS entity and an API operation pointing to the external endpoint 
  2. Admin adds the button on the UI via Adaptation — wires the button to the custom service action.

When the agent/user clicks the button, the framework calls the external API and resolves the parameter bindings (if defined while adding button) from the current entity context.

Part 1: Custom Service Configuration (Admin)

Step 1: Create an ACTIONPARAMETERS Entity

In the Custom Service metadata, define an entity of type ACTIONPARAMETERS. This entity also describes the input parameters the action expects as attributes.(optional)

Step 2: Define the API with an Action Operation

Define an API in the custom service metadata that references the ACTIONPARAMETERS entity and points to the external endpoint.

The apiPath points to the configured outbound connection for the custom service. The framework resolves this at runtime via the host configuration defined for the service.

 Configure entities and API via Metadata Creator and upload the JSON.

 

 

While defining API, provide entity reference to ActionParameters entity created above and add POST operation.

            "objectTypeCode": "CUS1538",

        }

}

Part 2: Adding the Button via Adaptation (Admin)

Once the custom service is configured, the next step is to surface the action as a button on the UI. This is done through Adaptation Mode.

Navigate to the relevant screen in the application and enter Adaptation Mode. Select the UI section where the button should appear and click Add Button. In this example, the button is added under the Actions column on the detail screen.

 

 

Fill in the mandatory fields. For Trigger Type, select Custom API. Then choose the relevant Custom Service and Action from the dropdowns. Click Apply to save the button configuration.

 

 

Runtime Behaviour

 

When the agent clicks the Cancel Change Start Date button:

  1. The framework detects the custom API Action configured on the respective button.
  2. It resolves all parameter bindings from the current entity instance data.
  3. It assembles the request body matching the ACTIONPARAMETERS entity shape.
  4. It issues a POST to the configured action endpoint.
  1. For this example, The CPI iFlow receives the call, processes it, and triggers the cancellation in S/4HANA.

Note: Clicking the button triggers the API in Fire and Forget mode — the call runs in the background and the UI remains unaffected.

This feature is currently available for custom UIs generated via Custom Services and the following standard applications: Contract Accounts, and Guided Selling. Support for additional standard applications will be available in future releases.

entry.title: Tired of Watching Claude? Make It Chirp.
entry.content:
The Problem

You're basically babysitting an AI If you use Claude Code for anything non-trivial like refactoring a module, generating test coverage, reworking a large prompt chain - you know the ritual. You kick off the task, switch windows, try to get other work done, then find yourself reflexively tabbing back every two minutes to check whether it's finished. It's the same anxiety loop as waiting for a CI pipeline, except the feedback loop is shorter and the temptation to check is even stronger.

Claude Code doesn't ship with a "notify me when done" button. So I built one.

What ClaudeChirp Does

ClaudeChirp is a pair of small shell scripts that plug into Claude Code's hook system. When a task finishes: A macOS Notification Center banner pops up - the title shows how long it ran and the body shows the first lines of Claude's own closing summary.

Optionally, a headless email lands in your Outlook inbox - no compose window, no focus steal, just a quiet message with the full summary and the duration. You configure a threshold (default: 5 minutes). Tasks shorter than the threshold are silently ignored.

You can also tell Claude per-task: "notify me when done" to force a notification, or "don't ping me" to suppress one.

How It Works

Claude Code supports lifecycle hooks, so shell commands that fire at key moments in a session:

UserPromptSubmit fires when you submit a prompt. ClaudeChirp uses this to record the current Unix timestamp for the session. Stop fires when Claude finishes a task. ClaudeChirp measures the elapsed time, extracts Claude's final message from the hook payload, and dispatches whichever notification channels are enabled. The Stop hook receives a JSON payload that includes the last assistants' message which is Claude's own summary of what it just did.

The email channel uses Outlook's AppleScript object model (tell application "Microsoft Outlook"), which is fully headless. No window opens, no focus changes, Outlook doesn't even come to the foreground. macOS prompts for Automation permission once on first run, and then it just works.

Six steps to set it up

Prerequisites: macOS, Claude Code, bash/python3/osascript (all pre-installed on macOS). Outlook only if you want the email channel.

  • git clone https://github.com/joshuasteinert/claudechirp
  • cd claudechirp
  • cp config.example ~/.claude/claudechirp/config
  • Edit config: set your email, threshold, and which channels to enable
  • ./install.sh

That's it. install.sh copies the hooks to ~/.claude/claudechirp/hooks and wires them into ~/.claude/settings.json. Restart Claude Code afterwards. Config file (~/.claude/claudechirp/config):

  • NOTIFY_EMAIL="" # required for mail channel
  • THRESHOLD_MINUTES=5 # only notify for tasks at least this long
  • NOTIFY_PING=1 # macOS Notification Center banner
  • NOTIFY_MAIL=1 # headless email via Outlook

You can use either channel independently so ping-only, mail-only, or both.

Verify it works

To verify whether the installation worked, you can set THRESHOLD_MINUTES to 0 and run any query in Claude Code. It should then send a ping or mail if enabled.

Try It

The project is on GitHub: https://github.tools.sap/I570066/ClaudeChirp.git

It's macOS-only for now (relies on osascript). It has no runtime dependencies beyond what ships with macOS. Install, configure, restart Claude Code and enjoy. If you use Claude Code for long-running tasks and find yourself switching back to check on it, this is the two-minute fix for that.

entry.title: Re: Suppressing output message for a changes done in crea...
entry.content:
Hi Atanas,

You don't need BRF+ for this. The rule that makes an item text change trigger a new PO output is customizing, and it is checked before BRF+ is even called. I read the code on S/4HANA 2023 and 2025 (the same code in both) and ran the check on 2023.

How the system decides

  • The class that triggers the output determination for purchase orders is CL_MM_PUR_PO_TRIGGER_OUTPUT. In method TRIGGER_OUTPUT_DETERMINATION, when the PO already has output, it first calls CHECK_CHANGES_OUTPUT_RELEVANT. If the answer is no, it returns before determining any new output item, so the BRF+ determination does not run for that save.
  • CHECK_CHANGES_OUTPUT_RELEVANT reads the change documents since the last output with ME_READ_CHANGES_EINKBELEG, print operation 2 (change). Inside, ME_CHANGES_PRINTOUT keeps only the changes that are relevant for printing. A field change counts when the table and field are in T166C. A text change counts when the text ID is in T166P for item texts, or T166K and T166A for header texts, for print operation 2, the document category, the document type and, for items, the item category.
  • No BAdI in that class. Confirmation changes (EKES) are ignored there.

What I ran

ME_CHANGES_PRINTOUT in memory, document type NB, print operation 2, one item text change, nothing saved:

  • F01, standard item category 0: 1 relevant change
  • F02, item category 0: 1
  • F05, item category 0: 0, because there is no T166P row for it
  • F02, item category 2: 0, because the delivered NB rows for category 2 have F01, F03 and F04 but not F02

In my system the delivered T166P rows for NB, print operation 2, item category 0 are EKPO F01, F02, F03, F04 and F10, EINE BT and MATERIAL BEST.

What you can do

  1. In T166P (DDIC text "Item Texts in Purchasing Document Printouts"), remove the row for print operation 2, category F, your document type, item category, object EKPO and the text ID your users change (F01 is the item text). After that, a save where only that text changed is not output relevant and no new PURCHASE_ORDER output item is created.
  2. Any other change that is in T166C still triggers the output as before.

What surprised me, and it is good news for you: the item texts printed on the PO form come from T166P with print operation 1 (new), and that is hard coded. CL_FDP_EF_PUR_ORD_FORM_UTILITY, method GET_ITEM_TEXTS, selects with "WHERE druvo EQ 1", and the form data provider CL_FDP_EF_PURCHASE_ORD_DPC_EXT calls it. So removing the print operation 2 row does not take the text out of the printout. The next output, triggered by a real change, still shows the current text.

About "choose": this check has no switch per save. It is per document type and item category, so it is the same for every user.

What I did not test: changing a real PO and saving it, the resulting output item in Output Management, and S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition.

entry.title: SAP at the Agentic AI Foundation: Shaping the Rules of Standardized AI
entry.content:
SAP joined the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) just days after its launch in December 2025 as a gold member. The thinking was simple: the rules for agentic AI are being written right now, and there's a real difference between being in the room from the very beginning than catching up later.

What is the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF)?

This Foundation was established in response to a growing demand for standardization, accessibility, and security of AI agents. AAIF brings together companies, researchers, and practitioners to define shared blueprints for agentic AI: things like taxonomy, reference architectures, and protocols that let agents communicate, identify themselves, and operate securely across organizational boundaries. Essentially, the scaffolding that makes multi-vendor agentic systems work.

Different working groups cover everything from identity & trust to security, workflows, observability, governance, and agentic commerce. SAP is most active in the Identity & Trust and Security working groups, areas where we've already been able to contribute best practices and guidance.

The foundation provides neutral governance for a growing number of protocols, including Model Context Protocol (MCP), Agent2Agent (A2A), and AGENTS.MD (full list on AAIF’s website).

SAP relies on protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol. While MCP standardizes the connection between models and external resources, A2A complements it by enabling autonomous, multi-turn collaboration between independent AI agents. This week, SAP published new architecture guidelines for integrating external AI agents with Joule (read more) and integrating Joule agents into a customer’s ecosystem (read more), describing outbound and inbound interoperability of external agents and applications with SAP ecosystem agents via the A2A protocol. This is just one example of how SAP uses some of the foundation’s major protocols.

Why SAP engages

The standards we help define today will determine whether tomorrow's agentic systems actually work in complex, regulated enterprise environments, and that's reason enough to show up. Contributing SAP use cases and enterprise requirements means these realities get built into the standards, not bolted on afterwards.

SAP experts from different areas have subscribed to the different working groups as soon as they were established earlier this year. Many of them joined the regular meetings although time-zone challenges sometimes make it hard to attend live. As of Sept. 2026, we ranked among the top three organizations in working group attendance.

In my role overseeing our engagement, we regularly revisit where it makes sense to invest time and effort. SAP co-leads the Identity & Trust working group, directly influencing how agent identity and delegation are defined industry wide.

Recent contributions in different areas

In the Identity and Trust working group, Alper Dedeoğlu (SAP OCTO, @alperdedeoglu18 ) co-authored the white paper "Agent Identity as Primitive", a foundational document defining how agent identity, delegation, and cross-organizational trust should be treated as first-class primitives in the agentic AI stack. It is currently under review by the AAIF Technical Committee and will be published in the working group's GitHub repository.

SAP leads two workstreams in the Security and Privacy working group. Fernando Lucktemberg from CAS Delivery drove the Agentic AI Security Best Practices Guide, offering structured guidance on secrets management, secure tool invocation, guardrails, and post-incident forensics. Alongside this, SAP contributed the Agentic AI Threat Modeling: Gap Analysis and Framework Design, identifying gaps in existing frameworks when applied to agentic systems, covering challenges like prompt injection, tool poisoning, and multi-agent trust.

Presence at conferences and in the community

SAP's engagement is also visible in the conference space. In September 2026, colleagues presented at AgntCon + MCPCon Amsterdam, hosted by the Agentic AI Foundation / LFX, on agent catalog discovery and how Open Resource Discovery addresses the challenge of finding the right MCP server among thousands of options (read more in related blog post How Companies Are Approaching MCP: Reflections Fro... - SAP Community). In October, SAP presented at the MCP Dev Summit in Toronto on building agentic systems that leverage MCP as a data connection layer.

On the community education side, the SAP Open Source Program Office hosted a public webinar on the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol in September 2026 and will offer further virtual learning sessions.

What comes next

Personally, I find this work motivating because it's rare to see open standards moving this fast in the enterprise space. We're still early, and there's more to do. Colleagues say that being part of shaping these standardization efforts, rather than adapting to them later, motivates them to engage in these discussions.

Don’t miss the webinar on Nov 18, 2026, hosted by the SAP Open Source Program Office with Alex Salkever (Editor-in-Chief of the AAIF Foundation) and Alper Dedeoğlu (Development Expert, SAP OCTO and Co-Chair of the AAIF Identity & Trust Working Group) and myself. Learn why open standards are critical for enterprise interoperability with agents, and how SAP engages with and contributes to the AAIF. In this live session, you can explore what the Identity & Trust Working Group is producing and why it matters for anyone building or deploying AI agents at scale (Link to registration page). Looking forward to seeing you in this virtual session and discussing agentic standardization with you.

We are already planning local meetups for 2027 together with the AAIF community. One will be at our SAP Labs in München Garching at the end of February (Events - Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF)).

  • Upcoming Webinar about our collaboration with the Agentic AI Foundation on Nov 18th
  • SAP Architecture Center with guidelines and architecture references on agentic AI
